evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Late stages of capacitation comprise intracellular alkalinization.
source: Late stages of capacitation comprise—amongst others—intracellular alkalinization (Meizel and Deamer, 1978), elevation of intracellular Ca2+ (Visconti et al., 2002), and membrane hyperpolarization (Zeng et al., 1995; Arnoult et al., 1996; Demarco et al., 2003).

claim: Slo channels possess seven transmembrane helices S0–S6.
source: These channels possess seven transmembrane helices S0–S6, with the S1–S6 helices exhibiting homology to classic voltage-gated K+ channels.

claim: Slo channels are tetramers of α subunits.

claim: The K+-selective pore of Slo channels is formed by S5 and S6.

claim: The Slo1 channel contains a large cytosolic C-terminus with two intracellular regulators of K+ conductance (RCK).
source: In addition, the Slo1 channel contains a large cytosolic C-terminus with two intracellular regulators of K+ conductance (RCK), both of which contain high affinity Ca2+ binding sites (Jiang et al., 2001; Yuan et al., 2010).

claim: Both RCK domains in Slo1 contain high affinity Ca2+ binding sites.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slo1 channels can sense changes in both voltage and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations.
source: These structural elements give Slo1 channels the ability to sense changes in both voltage and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations (Marty, 1981; Pallotta et al., 1981; Barrett et al., 1982; Latorre et al., 1982; Schreiber et al., 1999).

claim: Slo1 channels have a large single-channel conductance of 60–270 pS.

source: Slo1 is detectable in excitable tissues, such as in hippocampus (Hicks and Marrion, 1998), smooth muscle cells (Knaus et al., 1994a, 1994b) and adrenal chromaffin cells (Solaro and Lingle, 1992), whereas Slo3 transcripts are exclusively expressed in male germ cells (Schreiber et al., 1998).

claim: The molecular identity of human KSper is distinct from that of murine KSper.
